steps.stem: In a survey, 55% of people do not own a bicycle. Of the bicycle owners, 40% own an electric bicycle and the rest own only ordinary bicycles. What percentage of all surveyed people own only ordinary bicycles?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) people. \(55\) do not own a bicycle, so \(100-55=45\) own one.
The \(40\%\) is of the owners: \(10\%\) of \(45\) is \(4.5\), so \(40\%\) of \(45\) is \(4\times4.5=18\) electric.
Ordinary only: \(45-18=27\) people out of \(100\), so \(27\%\).

steps.title: Percentages to know
steps.intro: The fraction–percent table and the methods. Learn the table by heart.

tables.title: Methods
head: Method
When
Example
rows: building an equation; a letter inside the percent
quick; go straight to what they ask
percent of a percent, whole not given
visual version: multiply along the path

tips: The whole comes right after "of" / "than" — use the one in the question.
Each new percent sits on the NEW amount: \(+25\%\) then \(-20\%\) returns to the start.
Adding \(\frac1n\) and then removing \(\frac1{n+1}\) brings you back: \(+20\%\), \(-16\frac23\%\).
Any two changes \(a\%\) and \(b\%\): \(a+b+\frac{ab}{100}\) (a fall is negative). \(+25\), \(-20\) → \(25-20-5=0\).

steps.stem: A battery has used 72.5% of its original charge. What fraction remains?
A display item originally costs 760 credits. Its price is reduced by 75%. What is the new price?
explanation: A \(75\%\) reduction leaves \(100\%-75\%=25\%=\frac14\) of the price.

steps.stem: A membership fee rises from 60 credits to 66, then to 72. How do the two percentage increases compare?
choices: The first percentage increase is larger
The second percentage increase is larger
explanation: Same top, bigger bottom: \(\frac1{11}<\frac1{10}\). The first percentage increase is larger.

steps.stem: A player gives away 25% of her points. She then receives a bonus equal to 30% of the points she has left. Compared with her original score, what is her final score?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) points. Giving away \(25\%\) leaves \(75\).
With multipliers: \(0.75\times1.3=0.975\), which is \(97.5\%\) of the original.

steps.stem: A price rises by \(25\%\). Later, the new price falls by \(12\%\). By what percent is the final price higher than the original price?
explanation: Multipliers: up \(25\%\) is \(\times1.25\), and down \(12\%\) is \(\times0.88\).
\(1.25\times0.88=0.88+\frac14\times0.88=0.88+0.22=1.1\). The final price is \(110\%\) of the original: \(10\%\) higher.

steps.stem: Rae earns \(20\%\) more than Sol. Tia earns \(16\frac23\%\) less than Rae. What is Tia’s wage divided by Sol’s wage?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) for Sol. Rae earns \(20\%\) more: \(120\).
Tia’s wage divided by Sol’s wage: \(100\div100=1\).
\(22.5\%=3\times7.5\%\), so \(22.5\%\) of \(x\) is \(3\times12=36\). There is no need to find \(x\).

steps.stem: For \(x>0\), which expression is not equal to \(15\%\) of \(4x\)?
explanation: Every choice is also over \(100\), so compare the tops: \(10\cdot6x=60x\), \(60\cdot x=60x\), \(5\cdot12x=60x\), but \(30\cdot4x=120x\).
Since \(x>0\), \(120x\ne60x\). Only \(30\%\) of \(4x\) is not equal.

steps.stem: A workshop uses 80% of its timber on Monday and all the rest on Tuesday. Monday’s use is 36 planks greater than Tuesday’s. How many planks are used on Tuesday?
explanation: The difference is \(80\%-20\%=60\%\), and it equals \(36\) planks.

steps.stem: At the end of each hour, \(20\%\) of the water then in a tank is removed. After two hours, \(128\) liters remain. How many liters were there at the start?
explanation: Each hour \(20\%\) is removed, so \(80\%\) stays: multiply by \(0.8\).
After two hours: \(0.8\times0.8=0.64\), so \(64\%\) of the start remains.

steps.title: Percent traps and shortcuts
steps.intro: Three traps the exam loves, and two shortcuts that save time.

tables.title: Traps and shortcuts
head: Idea
Example
rows: Add water: the salt stays. \(20\) g salt \(=8\%\) → total \(250\) g
Letters in the choices: plug in numbers
What percent of \(a\) is \(b\)? \(a=50\), \(b=10\) → \(20\%\) → test each choice

tips: Plugging in numbers: not \(0\), not \(1\), and a different number for each letter.
If two choices give your target, choose new numbers and test only those two.

steps.stem: Last year, \(40\%\) of the students in a school passed a test. This year, \(50\%\) of the students passed. The number of students in the school did not change. By what percent did the number of students who passed increase?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) students. Last year \(40\) passed, and this year \(50\) passed.
The change is \(50-40=10\). Divide by the original: \(\frac{10}{40}=\frac14=25\%\).
The rate rose by \(10\) percentage points, but the number of students who passed rose by \(25\%\).

steps.stem: The price of a desk is \(150\%\) of the price of a chair. The price of a table is \(150\%\) more than the price of the chair. By what percent is the price of the table higher than the price of the desk?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) for the chair. The desk is \(150\%\) of \(100\): \(150\).
Compared with the desk: the change is \(250-150=100\), and \(\frac{100}{150}=\frac23=66\frac23\%\).

steps.stem: A \(300\)-gram mixture of sugar and water is \(20\%\) sugar. How many grams of sugar must be added to make the mixture \(40\%\) sugar?
explanation: Adding sugar does not change the water. Water: \(80\%\) of \(300\) is \(240\) g.

steps.stem: A school has \(N\) students, and \(g\) of them are girls. \(25\%\) of the girls play chess. What percent of all the students are girls who play chess?
explanation: Plug in numbers: \(N=200\) and \(g=80\). \(25\%\) of \(80\) girls is \(20\) girls who play chess.
In general: \(\frac g4\) girls play chess, and \(\frac{g}{4}\div N\times100=\frac{25g}{N}\).

steps.stem: What is \(75\%\) of \(\frac89\)?
A player hits a target on 40% of her attempts. She misses on 18 attempts. How many attempts does she make?
explanation: She hits on \(40\%\), so she misses on \(100\%-40\%=60\%\) of her attempts.

steps.stem: A tray holds 80 beads, each either white, purple, or orange. Half are white. Of the beads that are not white, 65% are purple. How many are orange?
explanation: White: half of \(80\) is \(40\). Not white: \(80-40=40\).
Purple is \(65\%\) of them, so orange is \(100\%-65\%=35\%\) of \(40\).

steps.stem: \(15\%\) of \(3x\) is \(18\). What percentage of \(x\) is \(18\)?
explanation: So \(18\) is \(45\%\) of \(x\). There is no need to find \(x\).

steps.stem: A town’s population grows from \(12{,}000\) to \(13{,}500\). What is the percentage increase?
A worker’s wage is 25% higher than a trainee’s wage. The trainee’s wage is what percentage lower than the worker’s?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) for the trainee, so the worker earns \(125\).
The trainee earns \(25\) less, measured against the worker: \(\frac{25}{125}=\frac15=20\%\).

steps.stem: \(75\%\) of a training group hold a certificate. Eighteen people hold only a first-aid certificate, and every other certificate holder holds only a coaching certificate. The number with coaching certificates equals the number with no certificate. How many people are in the group?
explanation: Coaching equals no certificate: \(25\%\). First aid: \(75\%-25\%=50\%\).

steps.stem: An allowance increases by 50%. The recipient then gives 20% of the new allowance to a sibling. The amount kept is what percentage of the original allowance?
explanation: \(120\) out of the original \(100\): \(120\%\). With multipliers: \(1.5\times0.8=1.2\).

steps.stem: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the overall change?
A bicycle’s new price is 40% above its original price. By what percentage must the new price fall so that it is only 12% above the original?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) for the original price. New price: \(140\). Target: \(112\).
The drop is \(140-112=28\). Measure it against the current price, \(140\): \(\frac{28}{140}=\frac15=20\%\).

steps.stem: An art box begins with equal numbers of blue and yellow chalk sticks. After half of all the sticks are used, 14 blue and 6 yellow remain. What percentage of the used sticks were yellow?
explanation: \(14+6=20\) sticks remain. That is half, so \(20\) were used and there were \(40\) at the start: \(20\) of each color.

steps.stem: In a college, laptop owners outnumber non-owners by 3 to 1. Of the laptop owners, 40% own a touch-screen laptop. What percentage of all students do not own a touch-screen laptop?
explanation: Owners to non-owners is \(3\) to \(1\), so owners are \(\frac34=75\%\) of the students.
Touch-screen owners: \(40\%\) of \(75\%\) is \(0.4\times75\%=30\%\) of all students.

steps.stem: After a 15% discount, a desk costs 306 credits. What was its original price?
explanation: The paid price is \(100\%-15\%=85\%\) of the original.

steps.stem: A shop offers either 30% off a 160-credit item or two successive discounts of 20% and 15%. How much cheaper is the two-discount option?
A coat is reduced from \(240\) credits to \(174\) credits. The discount is \(a\%\). Which interval contains \(a\)?

Given:
\(\begin{cases} a+b=200 \\ a=b+60 \end{cases}\)
What percentage of \(a+b\) is \(b\)?
A bank lowered its interest rate from \(5\%\) to \(4\%\). By what percent did the interest rate fall?
explanation: The rate fell by \(5-4=1\) percentage point.
In percent: change divided by the original, \(\frac15=20\%\).

steps.stem:
In January, \(20\%\) of the workers in a factory worked at night. In February, \(25\%\) of the same workers worked at night. Which of the following statements is true?
I. The share of night workers rose by \(5\) percentage points.
II. The number of night workers rose by \(25\%\).
explanation: II: plug in \(100\) workers. Night workers: \(20\to25\). The change is \(5\), and \(\frac5{20}=25\%\). True.

steps.stem: A club has 15 junior members. Juniors make up at least 25% and at most 75% of the club. What is the greatest possible number of senior members?
explanation: The more members the club has, the smaller the juniors’ share. So use the smallest share: \(25\%\).
\(15\) juniors \(=25\%=\frac14\) of the club, so the club has \(4\times15=60\) members.

steps.stem: Given: \(y>0\), and \(x\) is \(300\%\) more than \(y\). \(x\) is what percent of \(y\)?

A price was raised, and the new price was \(120\%\) of the original price. Later it was raised again, and it became \(150\%\) of the original price. By what percent was the price raised the second time?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) for the original price: \(100\to120\to150\).
The second rise is \(150-120=30\), measured against \(120\): \(\frac{30}{120}=\frac14=25\%\).
The trap: \(150-120=30\) percentage points is not \(30\%\).

steps.stem: A camera’s price rises by 10% in each of two years. The second-year price is 63 credits above the original price. What was the original price?
explanation: Two \(10\%\) rises: multiply by \(1.1\times1.1=1.21\). In total the price rises by \(21\%\).

steps.stem: The price of a coat was raised by \(20\%\). Then the new price was lowered by \(25\%\), and the coat now costs \(180\) credits. What was the original price?
explanation: Multipliers: \(1.2\times0.75=0.9\). The final price is \(90\%\) of the original.

steps.stem: The number of members in a club grows by \(10\%\) every year. By what percent does it grow over three years?
explanation: That is \(133.1\%\) of the start: a growth of \(33.1\%\).

steps.stem: Of the same savings balance, \(p\%\) is \(90\) credits and \(q\%\) is \(150\) credits. Which of the following is necessarily true?
explanation: Percents of the same whole are in the same ratio as their amounts: \(\frac pq=\frac{90}{150}=\frac35\).

steps.stem: A tablet is sold at a discount. Which information alone is not enough to find its original price?
choices: The discount percentage and the paid price
The ratio of the paid price to the original price
The discount percentage and the amount saved
The amount saved and the paid price
explanation: A ratio gives only the relative size, not an amount of credits. Paying \(\frac45\) of the price could be \(80\) out of \(100\) or \(160\) out of \(200\).
Each other choice gives at least one amount in credits, so the price can be found. For example, original price \(=\) amount saved \(+\) price paid.

steps.stem: A container holds \(300\) g of salt water that is \(20\%\) salt. How many grams of pure water must be added to make it \(15\%\) salt?
explanation: Adding water does not change the salt. Salt: \(20\%\) of \(300\) is \(60\) g.

steps.stem: A \(60\)-liter drink is \(25\%\) juice, and the rest is water. How many liters of water must be removed so that the drink becomes \(40\%\) juice?
explanation: Removing water does not change the juice: \(25\%\) of \(60\) is \(15\) liters.

steps.stem: \(20\) liters of a drink that is \(10\%\) juice are mixed with \(30\) liters of a drink that is \(20\%\) juice. What percent of the mixture is juice?
explanation: Juice: \(10\%\) of \(20\) is \(2\) liters, and \(20\%\) of \(30\) is \(6\) liters. Together: \(8\) liters.
The trap: \(15\%\) is the simple average, but there is more of the \(20\%\) drink.

steps.stem: A jacket is discounted by 36 credits. Its price after the discount is \(x\) credits. What is the discount percentage?
explanation: Change divided by the original, times \(100\): \(\frac{36}{x+36}\times100=\frac{3600}{x+36}\).
Check with a number: if \(x=64\), the original price is \(100\) and the discount is \(36\%\). \(\frac{3600}{64+36}=36\) ✓.

steps.stem: A museum has \(N\) visitors, of whom \(b\) bought an audio guide. The fraction of audio-guide buyers who chose English equals the fraction of all visitors who bought an audio guide. How many visitors chose an English guide?
explanation: Buyers are \(\frac bN\) of all visitors.
The same fraction of the \(b\) buyers chose English: \(b\times\frac bN=\frac{b^2}{N}\).

steps.stem: A library lends \(p\%\) of its books to Branch A, then lends \(p\%\) of the remaining books to Branch B, where \(0<p<100\). What is the ratio of the number sent to A to the number sent to B?
explanation: Plug in numbers: \(100\) books and \(p=50\). A gets \(50\), \(50\) remain, and B gets \(25\). The ratio is \(50:25=2:1\).
Check the choices with \(p=50\): only the ratio \(100:(100-p)=100:50=2:1\) fits.
In general: A gets \(\frac p{100}T\) and B gets \(\frac p{100}\cdot\frac{100-p}{100}T\). Their ratio is \(1:\frac{100-p}{100}=100:(100-p)\).

steps.stem: A number \(x>0\) is increased by \(p\%\), and the result is then decreased by \(p\%\). What is the final number?
explanation: Check with numbers: \(x=100\) and \(p=10\): \(100\to110\to99\). The choices give \(100\), \(81\), \(0\) and \(99\) ✓.

steps.stem: A subscription begins at \(96\) credits. After each annual review, its price rises by \(50\%\). After which review is its price first not a whole number of credits?
explanation: A \(50\%\) rise multiplies the price by \(1.5=\frac32\): times \(3\), divided by \(2\).
Each review uses up one factor \(2\). \(96=2^5\cdot3\) has five factors \(2\).
So reviews 1 to 5 give whole numbers: \(96\to144\to216\to324\to486\to729\), and \(729=3^6\) has no factor \(2\) left.
Review 6: \(729\times1.5=1093.5\). The first price that is not a whole number comes after review 6.
